benefits: Reads any X.509 certificate without installing openssl — paste and see everything.
Shows expiry and days remaining at a glance, so renewals never surprise you.
Decodes extensions (SAN, key usage, constraints) that raw openssl output buries in noise.
Computes the SHA-256 fingerprint for pinning or comparison.
Private keys are never involved — and your certificate never leaves the browser.

faqs.a: In most panels: your hosting or CDN dashboard shows the certificate with a view/download PEM option. On a server you control: openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -showcerts, then copy the -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE----- block. Paste that block here.
faqs.q: How do I get a certificate in PEM format?

faqs.a: PEM is base64-encoded DER wrapped in -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE----- headers — the text format this tool reads. DER is the raw binary form of the same data. If you have a .der/.cer binary file, convert it: openssl x509 -inform DER -in cert.cer -out cert.pem.
faqs.q: What is the difference between PEM and DER?

faqs.a: A self-signed certificate is signed by its own key instead of a public CA. Browsers don't trust it, so visitors see warnings. It's fine for local development and internal tools, but public sites need a CA-issued certificate (Let's Encrypt is free).

The Subject Alternative Name list: every hostname the certificate is valid for. Modern browsers ignore the CN field and check only SANs, so if your domain isn't listed there, visitors get a name-mismatch error even with a valid certificate.

The SHA-256 fingerprint is a hash of the whole certificate, often used for certificate pinning or to compare certificates across servers. Two certificates with the same fingerprint are byte-identical.
faqs.q: What is the SHA-256 fingerprint for?

faqs.a: Check three things: the notAfter date (is it expired?), the SAN list (is your domain there?), and the issuer (is it a trusted CA or self-signed?). This tool surfaces all three immediately.
faqs.q: My site shows a certificate error — what should I check?

ssl-certificate-decoder.formula:
Decoding steps used by this tool:
1. Extract base64 between -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE----- markers and decode to DER bytes.
2. Parse ASN.1 DER: Certificate = SEQUENCE { tbsCertificate, signatureAlgorithm, signatureValue }.
3. From tbsCertificate read: version, serialNumber, signature OID, issuer Name, validity (UTCTime/GeneralizedTime), subject Name, subjectPublicKeyInfo, extensions.
4. Map OIDs to names (signature algorithms, key types, curves, extensions).
5. SHA-256 fingerprint = hex( SHA256(DER bytes) ).
howTo: Get the certificate in PEM format (the -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE----- text block).
Paste the complete block into the box above — decoding starts instantly.
Read the summary: subject, issuer, validity dates, days remaining, and key details.
Check the SAN list covers your domain and the issuer is a trusted CA.
Compare the SHA-256 fingerprint with the one your server or CA reports.
keyFacts: X.509 certificates are ASN.1 DER-encoded documents; PEM is just base64 DER with header lines.
Every certificate carries: subject, issuer, serial number, validity window, public key, signature, and extensions.
The validity window (notBefore/notAfter) decides when browsers accept the certificate.
The SAN (Subject Alternative Name) extension lists the hostnames the certificate covers — browsers check this, not CN.
Extensions like Basic Constraints, Key Usage, and Extended Key Usage limit what the certificate may be used for.
The SHA-256 fingerprint uniquely identifies the certificate bytes — same fingerprint means identical certificates.

limitations: Decodes the certificate you paste — it cannot fetch a live server's certificate itself.
Does not validate the trust chain; a decodable certificate can still be untrusted.
Shows what the certificate claims; revocation (CRL/OCSP) status is not checked.
Unusual or proprietary extensions are listed by OID without a decoded value.

ssl-certificate-decoder.workedExample:
Sample: a self-signed test certificate for example.com, decoded by the tool:
1. Subject: CN=example.com, OU=Engineering, O=Example Tools Pvt Ltd, L=Mumbai, ST=Maharashtra, C=IN.
2. Issuer: identical to subject — flagged self-signed (browsers will not trust it).
3. Serial: 4C:E4:39:A9:0D:3C:DA:74:B1:CC:34:E5:79:74:4A:E9:D3:D6:97:39.
4. Signature algorithm: sha256WithRSAEncryption. Public key: RSA 2048-bit.
5. Valid from 2026-10-18 07:03:33 UTC to 2029-01-20 07:03:33 UTC — about 824 days remaining.
6. SAN: example.com, www.example.com.
7. Extensions: Subject Key Identifier, Authority Key Identifier, Basic Constraints CA:FALSE, Key Usage Digital Signature + Key Encipherment, Extended Key Usage TLS Web Server Authentication.
Reading: valid dates and SANs, but self-signed — fine for testing, not for a public site.
